questions.question: Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet agronomist, soaked and chilled winter wheat seed so that it could be sown in spring and still bear grain that summer, a treatment called vernalisation. He claimed that the change would be inherited. Which result would have borne out that claim?
questions.answer: Seed of chilled plants, sown unchilled in spring, bearing grain
choices: Seed of chilled plants, sown unchilled in spring, bearing grain
Seed of chilled plants, chilled again, sown in spring, bearing grain
Chilled seed, sown in spring, bearing grain the same summer
Unchilled winter wheat, sown in spring, bearing no grain that summer
questions.context: Only seed of chilled plants, sown in spring with no cold of its own, could show a change passed down; chill that seed again and the new cold explains the grain, while the other results tell only what cold does to the seed it touches. Plant biologists have since found that the chilled state is wiped clean as each new embryo forms, so every generation needs its own winter. Nikolai Vavilov, the country's leading plant scientist, at first encouraged Lysenko's work and stopped when it failed to deliver.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks which result would test a claim, and an inherited change can only be tested in the offspring, not in the plant that was treated.

questions.question: Trofim Lysenko denied that genes existed and rejected Gregor Mendel's laws of heredity. N. I. Ermolaeva, whose work Lysenko backed, repeated some of Mendel's pea crosses and reported in 1939 that her counts showed Mendel's ratio of 3 to 1 to be false. The mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov went through her counts in 1940. What did he find?
questions.answer: They strayed from 3 to 1 no more than chance allows
choices: They strayed from 3 to 1 no more than chance allows
They strayed from 3 to 1 further than chance allows
They kept closer to 3 to 1 than chance allows
They kept closer to a ratio of 1 to 1 than to 3 to 1
questions.context: Real counts never land exactly on 3 to 1, any more than a hundred coin tosses land exactly fifty-fifty, and Kolmogorov showed that her counts scattered around Mendel's ratio as widely as chance predicts, no more and no less, calling them a new confirmation of Mendel's laws. Lysenko held that Kolmogorov was wrong; he also claimed that mathematics had no place in biology. Two researchers who rechecked the work in 2011 found flaws in Kolmogorov's method, yet a corrected test still confirmed his conclusion.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn that measurements vary by chance and that data are judged against that variation, not against an exact figure.

questions.question: Trofim Lysenko's attack on genetics won the day at the August 1948 session of the Soviet academy of farm science, with Joseph Stalin's approval. In the months that followed, an order went out to destroy all the stocks of one living thing that geneticists kept for their research. Which living thing did the order name?
choices: Fruit flies
Pea plants
Lab mice
Maize plants
questions.context: The order named Drosophila, the fruit fly, one of the creatures genetics labs most often bred to study heredity. After the session genetics was barred from teaching and research, and more than 3,000 biologists were dismissed or jailed; Soviet leaders had wanted Lysenko's quick promises after the famine of the early 1930s, when breeding by genetics looked slow. The ban was lifted only in the mid-1960s, after his methods had failed in the fields and he lost his posts.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches the fruit fly as the classic animal of genetics labs, and the order to destroy its stocks shows a state wiping out the tools of a science it had banned.

questions.question: Crews planting forest belts across the Soviet steppes under a plan of 1948 sowed acorns in tight clusters, Trofim Lysenko's 'nests', for he held that seedlings of one kind crowded together help one another. The ecologist Vladimir Sukachev, an opponent of Lysenko, recorded that by September 1951 every tree planted by the nest method in the Ural lands had died. Which planting, compared with the nests, would have shown whether the crowding was to blame?
questions.answer: Oaks sown singly on the same ground in the same years
choices: Oaks sown singly on the same ground in the same years
Oaks sown singly in a wetter land far away
Oaks sown in nests on the same ground a year later
Pines sown in nests on the same ground in the same years
questions.context: Only a planting that differs from the nests in crowding alone can single the crowding out: oaks sown singly in a wetter land might thrive for the water's sake, and the dry steppe or a bad run of weather could have killed nested and single trees alike. Critics of the method blamed the crowding, since seedlings of one kind need the same light, water and soil nutrients, and packing them together sharpens their competition. Across the whole plan, by one estimate, only about a tenth of the trees planted survived.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science asks what a control rules out, and only a planting that differs from the nests in crowding alone could test the claim the nests were built on.

questions.question: Nikolai Vavilov, the Soviet Union's leading plant scientist, led expeditions to five continents in the 1920s and 1930s and built in Leningrad the largest collection of crop seeds of its day. He sought out old local varieties and the wild relatives of crops, not only the best modern kinds. Why did he want those?
questions.answer: They held traits breeders could cross into new crops
choices: They held traits breeders could cross into new crops
They could be trained by cold to grow well on any farm
They stayed alive in storage far longer than modern seed
They gave bigger harvests than the modern varieties did
questions.context: Vavilov judged that modern crops, bred to be alike, were too uniform to withstand new diseases and hard seasons, while old local kinds and wild relatives hold the variety of genes, for traits such as resistance to drought and pests, that breeders can cross back in; he had wanted since boyhood to end famine. The secret police arrested him in 1940, while he was collecting seeds in Ukraine, for opposing Lysenko, and he died of starvation in Saratov prison in 1943. Through the siege of Leningrad his institute's staff guarded the collection, and some of them starved rather than eat it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade biology teaches genetic variation as the raw material of breeding and selection, and Vavilov's collection is the classic seed bank built on that idea.

questions.question: Charles Davenport's Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, worked to advance eugenics, the plan to improve future generations by stopping people judged 'unfit' from having children. Its field workers went door to door from 1910 to chart family trees. Where 'feeblemindedness' or pauperism turned up in parents and their children, the office counted it as inherited, often through a single gene. What could such a family tree never sort out?
questions.answer: Whether genes or a shared home and upbringing caused it
choices: Whether genes or a shared home and upbringing caused it
Whether the trait passed through the mother or the father
Whether the trait skipped a generation and came back
Whether more sons than daughters showed the trait
questions.context: Davenport, funded by Mary Harriman and later the Carnegie Institution, treated human traits as Mendelian 'unit characters', as the new genetics seemed to allow; but a family shares its home, food, schooling and poverty as well as its genes, so a trait that runs in a family does not by itself show that genes carry it, and Davenport also studied the genetics of pellagra, which proved to come from a vitamin missing in the diet. Critics of the day, among them Thomas Hunt Morgan and Herbert Spencer Jennings, argued that he overlooked the surroundings and that most human traits depend on many genes. 'Feebleminded' was a loose label for many conditions with many causes, and intelligence is now known to be shaped by a great many genes, each with a small effect, as well as by upbringing.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade investigation design teaches confounding variables, and a shared family environment is the confound the eugenic family trees never controlled.

questions.question: Harry Laughlin, superintendent of the Eugenics Record Office, gave a Virginia court his sworn expert judgement in 1924 in the case of Carrie Buck, a young woman held at the state colony for the 'feebleminded'. He called her family part of 'the shiftless, ignorant, and worthless class of anti-social whites of the South' and judged her condition inherited. What was his judgement based on?
questions.answer: What the colony's doctors had told him
choices: What the colony's doctors had told him
His own tests of her mind at the colony
The record of her lessons kept by her school
His own talks with the Bucks' neighbours
questions.context: Laughlin had never met Carrie Buck: the historian Paul Lombardo found that his statement repeated language the colony's doctors had given him, and it echoed what the colony's superintendent, Albert Priddy, had said of the family; it was read into the record in his absence. A teacher of hers had written that she was 'very good' in 'deportment and lessons' before she was taken out of school in sixth grade to do housework. Indiana had passed the first sterilisation law in 1907, and Virginia's law of 1924, which Priddy chose this case to test, followed a model law that Laughlin had drafted.
questions.grade_note: Ninth graders learn to judge a claim by the evidence behind it, and an expert's sworn word with no observation behind it is the clearest case of evidence that is not there.

questions.question: At the hearing on Carrie Buck in 1924, a social worker said that her baby daughter, Vivian, had 'a look about it that is not quite normal'. Arthur Estabrook of the Eugenics Record Office testified that Vivian had failed the usual test for a baby of about six months. The Supreme Court upheld Carrie's sterilisation in 1927, counting Vivian as a third generation. What did Vivian's school record later show?
questions.answer: A place on the honour roll in first grade
choices: A place on the honour roll in first grade
A grade skipped for her quick reading
A prize for arithmetic in her second year
A move to a special class for slow learners
questions.context: Vivian was placed on the honour roll in April 1931, and Stephen Jay Gould, who studied her school records, called her 'a perfectly normal, quite average student'; she died of an infection at eight in 1932. A social worker's remark and one failed test of a baby of about seven months stood as the evidence for the third generation in Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes's line, 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough.' California alone sterilised about 20,000 people under such laws, and the Court has never expressly overturned the case.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science teaches that a claim must survive later evidence, and Vivian's school record is the later evidence the eugenic judgement of a baby failed.

questions.question: Twenty doctors and three officials of Nazi Germany were tried at Nuremberg for medical experiments on prisoners of war and civilians, many of whom died. The three American judges set out ten principles for experiments on people in their verdict of August 1947. The opening sentence of the first principle calls one thing absolutely essential. What is it?
questions.answer: The voluntary consent of the person tested
choices: The voluntary consent of the person tested
Tests on animals before any test on people
Results that no other method could give
A risk no greater than the good it may do
questions.context: The first principle opens 'The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential' and goes on that the person must be free of 'force, fraud, deceit, duress' and know enough for 'an understanding and enlightened decision', a duty that falls on every person who starts, directs or works on the experiment. Animal tests first, results no other method can give and a risk no greater than the problem's importance are the Code's third, second and sixth principles. Several of the accused had argued that no law marked off a lawful experiment from an unlawful one; the Code itself was never made a law, but later codes of research ethics were modelled on it.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science includes the safe and ethical conduct of research, and the Nuremberg Code's first principle is the root of informed consent.

questions.question: The judges at Nuremberg set out ten principles for experiments on people in 1947. The ninth concerns a volunteer who, partway through an experiment, reaches a state of body or mind in which going on seems to him impossible. What does the ninth principle say of him?
questions.answer: He may stop, with no one's leave needed
choices: He may stop, with no one's leave needed
He may stop once the doctor in charge agrees
He may stop, but must give his reasons in writing
He may stop if a doctor judges that going on would injure him
questions.context: The ninth principle says that the subject 'should be at liberty to bring the experiment to an end if he has reached the physical or mental state where continuation of the experiment seems to him to be impossible': his own sense of his state is enough, with no doctor's leave, no reasons owed and no proof of harm. The tenth puts a duty on the scientist in charge as well, who must be ready to stop the experiment if he has cause to believe that going on is likely to injure, disable or kill the subject.
questions.grade_note: Ninth-grade science includes the ethical conduct of research on people, and a volunteer's freedom to stop, first set down in the Code's ninth principle, is a basic rule of it.

1bffdd959e.why: Judge (medium): 'He went further than the plants he treated' pointed beyond the treated seed, and the key was the only choice about offspring, so the T5 step (the offspring must go unchilled) was never tested. The clause is gone, and 'a bigger harvest' is replaced by 'Seed of chilled plants, chilled again, sown in spring, bearing grain', so two choices concern the offspring and only the unchilled one tests the claim.

82cc3fa48a.why: Judge (medium): two lures (blending, acquired traits) were rival theories, not results a check of pea counts could give, leaving two live choices. They are now count-shaped: 'strayed further than chance allows' (Ermolaeva's own claim) and 'kept closer to 3 to 1 than chance allows' (Kolmogorov found the scatter just as wide as chance predicts, F39). Judge (low): 'one of his followers' is now 'whose work Lysenko backed'. The key now reads 'no more than chance allows', so it is not the longest choice and pairs with 'further than'. Fact-check (error): 'bourgeois formalism' is not a documented Lysenko quotation (F43); the card now says, unquoted, that he claimed mathematics had no place in biology (F4).

4c4fbf023d.why: Judge (medium): once the stem said Stalin and the Party's Central Committee approved Lysenko's report, suppression was the only believable answer, and the key was a political act (the history bank's lane). Re-keyed, as the judge proposed, on the science destroyed: the order to destroy all stocks of Drosophila (F36, Wikipedia citing Medvedev). The question asks only which living thing the ORDER named, since Borinskaya 2019 says other mutant strains were also destroyed; the ban and the 3,000 dismissed moved to the card. 'kept for their research', not 'bred in their labs', so the two plant lures are not ruled out.

a6bd002c5c.why: Judge (medium): the key was a historical record, and 'most nests kept one strong tree' was what the ecology predicts, so knowing the science pushed a player wrong; the crowding science itself is the T2 carrot fact. Re-aimed, as the judge proposed, at the T5 step: which planting would test whether crowding was to blame. Key: oaks sown singly on the same ground in the same years; one lure varies crowding AND place (a confounded control), two keep the nests. Fact-check (uncertain): no source says Sukachev followed the plantings; the stem now says only that he recorded the loss (Wikipedia), and the card says critics blamed the crowding rather than stating it as proven (F37).

cdf1d77ec1.why: Judge (low): in a unit about a state that denied genes, the key was the only choice saying 'genes'; it is now 'They held traits breeders could cross into new crops'. Judge and fact-check (low): the collection was the largest 'of its day' (F16), and the stem now says so.

03fd123e17.why: Judge (medium): the word eugenics, the unit's subject, was never taught in any stem or card. The stem now defines it (F38: the selection of heritable traits to improve future generations, by stopping those judged unfit from having children). Key and choices unchanged.

362a80cd83.why: Judge (low): 'sent a sworn written statement' hinted that he was never there, weakening the two 'His own...' lures; it is now 'gave a Virginia court his sworn expert judgement'. Judge (low, stance): the card now names Albert Priddy, the colony's superintendent, whose statements Laughlin repeated and who chose this case to test the law (F42). Key and choices unchanged.

6ec6415834.why: Fact-check (uncertain): every source hedges the coin, and the Library of Virginia says her foster mother, Mrs. Dobbs, waved it, not Estabrook (F41). The stem now says only what is documented: Estabrook testified that Vivian had failed the usual test for a baby of about six months; the card drops the coin too. Judge (low): 'An intelligence score in the lowest tenth' is replaced by a second positive lure, 'A prize for arithmetic in her second year' (false: she earned a C in arithmetic, F29).

2242f92685.why: Judge (low): 'The first principle opens with a single sentence' was padding; the stem now says the first principle's opening sentence calls one thing absolutely essential. Key and choices unchanged.

added.cdbd26a180: Replaces the dropped fifth-principle question, as the judge proposed: the Code's ninth principle, a volunteer's liberty to end an experiment when going on seems to him impossible (F34, F40, the Avalon text). The stem carries the principle's condition, as the fact-check asked; the lures are a doctor's leave, written reasons and a doctor's finding of injury, none of which the text requires.

dropped.question: The fifth of the ten principles that the Nuremberg judges set out in 1947 bars any experiment on people where there is reason to expect, beforehand, that death or disabling injury will follow. The judges added a single exception to it, hedged with the word 'perhaps'. Which experiments does the exception cover?
dropped.why: Judge (high, grade): the self-experimenter exception to the fifth principle is a fine detail of a legal text met in college bioethics, and 'already have a deadly disease' looked as plausible to a 9th-grader as the key, so the question was a guess. Replaced by the ninth principle.

lead_edits.old: He is free to bring the experiment to an end
lead_edits.new: He may stop, with no one's leave needed
lead_edits.why: recheck: the key alone did not open 'He may stop', so it stood out
